items.title: Wendy Oxenhorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 22, 2026
items.q: I contacted a friend of mine and he was teaching African studies in – oh I forgot the university, Adam Gusso, but he was an amazing guy. He also played harmonica with an all-blues band. And he sent one of his students...

ctx.x: Yeah, right. And Milt Hinton and these fellas who played on these rock & roll records and all that, the story is completely fascinating to me.

It’s beyond. And we know all the earlier racism, everyone knows the clubs, the labels, the record companies, we know so many things that went down back then. There was one story that really stands out in my early moments, and I’ll segue into the Great Night in Harlem and answer your question, but there was a legend who – I think it was Ron Carter who came to me and said, “I ran into someone at the airport and he didn’t have a seeing eye cane but he was blind as a bat, he really couldn’t see where he was going.”…

coming back and I introduced him, I asked him to do a gig with this young musician and they got tight. And before we knew it young musicians were asking him to sit in at clubs. So he would guest star. So he was making money. They were getting paid more because they had the famous name and they were becoming like family. So this became a little thing that started happening with some of the elders. So many beautiful things. So okay, Great Night in Harlem. I really didn’t know anything about jazz. In fact I could…

items.title: Wendy Oxenhorn — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: The one man who gave me a harmonica lesson, this great guy, Adam Gussow, was teaching there

ctx.x: So you started very proactively making phone calls and...

Well, you’d hear about... Sure. Someone would tell me someone is having a hard time, and then that person would generally know someone, and then they would know someone. We got to all be so close, and it was such a feeling of family and of trust. It was a beautiful thing. I want to introduce Lauren Roberts to this. She was a 22-year-old Vassar student, who was just graduating. The one man who gave me a harmonica lesson, this great guy, Adam Gussow, was teaching there, and he was now moving to Mississippi, and he…
You were learning on the job, as seems to be what you’ve done all through your life and in your many activities.
